quote: wie viel Schnittflächen müssen gelegt werden, damit im so zerschnitt. Raum jede geschlossne Curve sich auf 0 zu- sammenziehn lässt
english: How many cut surfaces must be laid so that in the space thus cut every closed curve can be contracted to 0?
topic: Defines a first and second genus (p_1, p_2) of a space by the number of cut surfaces needed so that every closed surface, respectively every closed curve, can be contracted to a point, raises the existence problem for algebraic configurations with a prescribed branching scheme (a generalisation of Riemann's existence theorem), and lists coloured relations between three functions U, V, W.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a new research question. It restates the Riemann–Betti 'connectivity numbers' (Zusammenhangszahlen) for a 3-dimensional space or manifold M: what is the minimum number of non-separating cut surfaces needed so that, in what remains of M after cutting, every closed curve can be shrunk to a point? Hilbert's 'second genus' p_2 asks this for closed curves. In modern terms it is the cut-based version of the first Betti number (equivalently, by Poincaré duality, the count of non-separating surfaces, b_2 = b_1 for a closed orientable 3-manifold). The note also mixes two ideas. Counting cuts measures homology, but asking that every curve shrink to a point is a statement about the fundamental group π_1. Poincaré later showed these two are not the same.
triage.answered_by: This was background theory, not an open problem. Riemann (the posthumous 'Fragment on Analysis Situs') and Betti (1871) had already defined these connectivity numbers. Poincaré turned them into Betti numbers in Analysis Situs (1895) and its supplements (1899–1904), introduced the fundamental group (1892), and Heegaard criticized his account (1898). Poincaré's homology sphere (1904) shows that knowing the Betti numbers (the cut count) does not tell you whether every curve can be contracted. The question 'when is a closed 3-manifold with trivial π_1 a 3-sphere' became the Poincaré conjecture. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems.

evidence.claim: Betti built on Riemann's idea of connectivity of surfaces to define connectivity numbers P1, P2, ..., now called Betti numbers. P2 counts disjoint closed surfaces in M that do not separate M.
In an undated 'Fragment on Analysis Situs' found among his papers, Riemann defined n-dimensional connectedness of a manifold using cuts.
Betti numbers count the 'cuts' (by curves, surfaces, etc.) that are needed. In 1892 Poincaré introduced the fundamental group, which refines the Betti numbers.
Poincaré's homology sphere has the same homology as the 3-sphere but a non-trivial fundamental group (fifth complement, 1904).
Heegaard (1898) criticized Betti's and Poincaré's definitions, and Poincaré answered in his 1899 Complément.
The Poincaré conjecture says a closed, connected 3-manifold with trivial fundamental group is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.

triage.why: On this page Hilbert uses the question to define p_1 and p_2 (genus via cut surfaces). That is the classical Riemann–Betti connectivity number, which Betti numbers and homology later made precise. Poincaré's work also settled the subtle point inside the question: cut counts (homology) do not decide whether every curve contracts (π_1). The basic definition is standard textbook topology and not an active research topic. Related questions did lead into long research programs, notably the Poincaré conjecture, proved by Perelman. Confidence is medium rather than high because no source discusses this exact diary note. The match rests on its wording and its period (the 1890s, before Poincaré's papers).
